== Glossary

[cols="1,3", options="header"]
|===
|Term |Definition

|ADR |Architecture Decision Record — a short document capturing a significant architectural choice, the context that prompted it, and the alternatives considered
|Audit Ledger |An append-only, tamper-evident log of every state transition within the platform; the digital equivalent of the paper trail currently maintained through email exchanges
|CAPEX |Capital Expenditure — one-time development and infrastructure setup costs
|Counterparty |An independent insurance company that holds one or more reinsurance contracts with the client; a fully separate legal entity and external tenant on the platform
|Eligibility |The determination of which individuals in a monthly data file fall within the risk coverage of a given contract, triggering a reinsurance compensation obligation
|Hash Chain |A sequence of SHA-256 hashes where each entry incorporates the hash of the previous entry; any tampering with a historical record breaks the chain and is immediately detectable
|Longevity Risk |The financial risk borne by an insurer when insured individuals outlive actuarial expectations, requiring continued pension or annuity payments beyond the projected period
|MFA |Multi-Factor Authentication — a login requirement for a second verification step (e.g. OTP) beyond a password; required for all platform users
|MoSCoW |Prioritisation framework: Must have / Should have / Could have / Won't have
|OPEX |Operational Expenditure — recurring monthly costs for infrastructure, managed services, and licences
|Pension Portfolio |A batch of insured individuals covered under a single longevity or pension reinsurance contract, tracked as a unit in the reconciliation process
|PRA |Prudential Regulation Authority — UK regulator overseeing insurance and reinsurance firms' capital adequacy
|Reconciliation Cycle |The monthly (or periodic) end-to-end process: counterparty submits data file → reinsurer calculates eligibility → both parties negotiate and sign off on compensation
|Reinsurance |Insurance sold to insurance companies; when an insurer faces excessive longevity or pension risk, it offloads part of that risk to a reinsurer in exchange for premium payments
|RLS |Row-Level Security — a PostgreSQL feature that enforces per-tenant data access at the database layer, preventing one counterparty from accessing another's records
|Solvency II |EU/UK regulatory framework governing insurance and reinsurance capital adequacy; requires auditable, long-term records of all risk transfer transactions
|Application State Machine |A workflow state machine implemented within the Approval Workflow module; the `workflow_state` column on `reconciliation_cycles` tracks each cycle through defined states; no external orchestration service required at current scale
|TCO |Total Cost of Ownership — full cost including development, infrastructure, and ongoing operations over a defined period
|Tenant |A single counterparty organisation on the platform; each tenant's data is strictly isolated from all other tenants
|===

== Executive Summary

=== Context

A UK-based reinsurance firm manages longevity and pension risk contracts with multiple independent insurance company counterparties. Each month, counterparties submit data files listing insured individuals still alive; the reinsurer's team applies contract rules to determine compensation, then both parties exchange proposals, negotiate adjustments, and sign off — entirely through email and Excel spreadsheets.

This manual process requires a large team of reconciliation managers. Trust between independent entities is established through repeated human verification. The client's innovation strategy seeks to automate this inter-company reconciliation, replacing manual labour with a verifiable, auditable digital platform — targeting a 2–4× reduction in reconciliation headcount while meeting UK FCA and Solvency II record-keeping obligations.

|===

=== Scope Boundary

This engagement delivers: contract registry with file type configuration, typed multi-file counterparty ingestion with per-counterparty file normalisation, expression tree-based eligibility engine with exact decimal arithmetic, multi-level approval workflow with counter-proposal support, immutable audit ledger, multi-tenant web portal, counterparty onboarding, email notifications, data residency zone tracking, and regulatory export.

This engagement explicitly *does not* include: payment service provider integration (B2B money settlement is handled outside the platform), blockchain infrastructure, historical Excel record migration (closed cycles remain in existing archives), consumer-facing functionality, or changes to the counterparties' internal systems.

=== Key Decisions

[cols="1,3,1,1"]
|===
|# |Decision |Chosen Approach |Reversibility

|1
|How to achieve immutability and tamper-evidence without blockchain
|PostgreSQL append-only audit table with SHA-256 hash chain
|Hard — changing the audit model requires data migration

|2
|How to orchestrate the multi-step, multi-level approval workflow
|Application-layer state machine with `workflow_state` column; background job handles escalation timers; extractable to Step Functions if workflow count grows
|Medium — state machine interface is a clean module boundary; extraction is additive

|3
|How to enforce multi-tenant data isolation
|PostgreSQL Row-Level Security (RLS) scoped per tenant
|Medium — switching to schema-per-tenant is a schema migration

|4
|How to authenticate external counterparty users
|AWS Cognito User Pool with mandatory MFA
|Easy — Cognito can be replaced without changing business logic

|5
|How counterparties exchange files with the platform
|HTTPS web upload via S3 pre-signed URLs; SFTP available as fallback; typed multi-file ingestion per cycle
|Easy — adding new exchange channels does not change core processing

|6
|How to handle compute for a monthly-peak workload
|Single ECS Fargate service (modular monolith) fronted by an Application Load Balancer + Aurora Serverless v2
|Medium — modular monolith boundaries allow extraction to separate services if warranted

|7
|How to express contract rules without per-contract code changes
|Structured expression tree (AND/OR/range/tiered) evaluated by a generic engine; validated against versioned JSON Schema
|Medium — rule schema is versioned; adding new node types is additive

|8
|How to handle diverse counterparty file formats
|Per-counterparty file normalisation mappings applied between raw upload and eligibility engine input; mappings stored as tenant configuration
|Easy — adding a new mapping does not change the engine or core schema

|9
|How to handle cross-cycle adjustments
|Snapshot-based: each adjustment triggers a full eligibility recalculation; results are self-contained, not deltas
|Medium — switching to delta-based requires engine changes and audit payload redesign

|10
|Which contract rule version applies when rules change mid-cycle
|Contract version locked at cycle opening; mid-cycle changes apply to the next cycle only
|Easy — policy decision, not a structural constraint
|===

== Problem Statement

=== Current Pain Points

[cols="1,3,2"]
|===
|# |Problem |Business Impact

|1
|All reconciliation work is performed manually via Excel and email; no shared digital workspace
|{current-headcount}+ reconciliation managers required; cost scales linearly with counterparty portfolio growth

|2
|No shared digital trust layer — trust between independent counterparties is established entirely through human verification
|Process cannot be automated; each new counterparty multiplies headcount proportionally

|3
|Multi-round email exchange: propose → dispute → adjust → re-send; no formal state tracking
|Cycle duration measured in weeks; errors discovered late cause expensive adjustment rounds

|4
|No tamper-evident audit trail — compliance evidence requires reconstructing email threads and Excel version histories
|Solvency II and FCA audit preparation is manual, slow, and dependent on individual employees

|5
|Contract formula knowledge is concentrated in undocumented Excel files held by specific individuals
|Key-person risk; staff departures could make rule logic irreproducible

|6
|No structured onboarding process for new counterparties
|Each new counterparty requires weeks of manual coordination and custom file format handling

=== Target State

A single cloud-hosted platform where the reinsurer acts as the trusted custodian. Counterparties log in, upload monthly data files through a secure portal, and review eligibility proposals computed automatically against their contract rules. A structured approval workflow replaces email chains. Every file upload, calculation, approval, and sign-off is recorded in an immutable audit ledger — providing Solvency II-grade compliance evidence without manual reconstruction.

|**Approach**
|Web portal + PostgreSQL audit triggers; manual approval via email prompts
|Application-layer state machine + dual-layer audit (S3 Object Lock + hash-chain) + multi-level approval workflow; ECS Fargate modular monolith + Aurora Serverless v2; exact decimal arithmetic required for financial precision
|Full event sourcing; every state transition stored as an immutable event; current state derived by replaying the event log

|**Immutability**
|DB-level insert triggers (weak — can be disabled by a DBA)
|Hash-chain audit table with SHA-256 (strong — tamper detection without DB-level enforcement)
|Event store is the system of record (strongest — true immutability by architecture)

|Manual (notification email → user acts → repeat)
|Application-layer state machine with `workflow_state` column; background job for escalation timers

|5–50 (covers full initial book)

|Manual SQL export

== Option 1: Lightweight Portal

=== Overview

[cols="1,2"]
|===
|Timeline |{opt1-timeline} months
|CAPEX |{opt1-capex-approx} (incl. 25% contingency)
|OPEX / month |{opt1-opex}

|Counterparty scale |Up to 5
|Audit strength |DB-level insert triggers (limited)
|===

=== What It Delivers

* Secure web portal with Cognito authentication and basic RBAC
* S3 file upload with SHA-256 checksum verification
* PostgreSQL database with audit triggers recording all inserts/updates
* Email-prompted approval (SES notification → user opens portal → approves manually)
* Basic regulatory export via SQL query

=== What It Doesn't

* Structured approval state machine — the process still relies on email discipline
* Hash-chain tamper detection — audit triggers can be bypassed by a DBA
* Automated eligibility calculation — a future investment
* Scale beyond 5 counterparties without significant re-architecture

=== Reconciliation Cycle Flow

Each monthly reconciliation cycle follows four phases. The workflow is managed by the application-layer state machine; every state transition is recorded as an immutable audit ledger event.

.Monthly Reconciliation Cycle — Four-Phase Flow
[plantuml,case03-cycle-flow,format=svg]
....
@startuml
skinparam backgroundColor #fafafa
skinparam defaultFontName Arial
skinparam defaultFontSize 14
skinparam activityBackgroundColor #E3F2FD
skinparam activityBorderColor #1565C0
skinparam arrowColor #1565C0

|Counterparty|
start
:Upload typed data files\n(people table, money movement,\nspecial conditions, etc.);

|Platform|
:Normalise files to\ncanonical schema;
:Check cycle readiness:\nall required file types received?;

if (All files present?) then (yes)
  :Trigger eligibility\ncalculation;
else (no)
  :Wait for remaining files;
  stop
endif

:Evaluate expression tree rules\nagainst all data files;
:Produce eligibility result\nand compensation proposal;

|Reinsurer|
:L1 Reconciliation Manager\nreviews proposal;

if (Approved?) then (yes)
  if (Amount > threshold?) then (yes)
    :L2 Senior Manager review;
  else (no)
  endif
else (request adjustment)
  |Counterparty|
  :Accept adjustment /\nsubmit revised file /\nsubmit counter-proposal;
  |Platform|
  :Re-trigger eligibility\nif data revised;
  |Reinsurer|
  :Review updated proposal;
endif

|Counterparty|
:Counter-sign cycle;

|Platform|
:Seal cycle in audit ledger\n(SHA-256 hash chain — immutable);
stop

@enduml
....

=== Approval Workflow State Machine

The approval model supports multi-round negotiation between the reinsurer and counterparty. The L1 reconciliation manager reviews each proposal; cycles above a configurable compensation threshold require L2 senior manager sign-off. Counterparties can submit revised data files at any point before the cycle is sealed — re-triggering a full eligibility recalculation — or issue a formal counter-proposal.

.Reconciliation Cycle — State Machine (Key States)
[plantuml,case03-state-machine,format=svg]
....
@startuml
skinparam backgroundColor #fafafa
skinparam defaultFontName Arial
skinparam defaultFontSize 14
skinparam state {
  BackgroundColor #E3F2FD
  BorderColor #1565C0
  ArrowColor #1565C0
  StartColor #1565C0
  EndColor #B71C1C
}

[*] --> Awaiting_Files : Cycle opened

Awaiting_Files --> Eligibility_Running : All required file\ntypes received

Eligibility_Running --> Reinsurer_Review : Calculation complete\n(L1, then L2 if threshold exceeded)

Reinsurer_Review --> Adjustment_Loop : Reinsurer requests adjustment
Adjustment_Loop --> Eligibility_Running : Counterparty submits\nrevised data file
Adjustment_Loop --> Reinsurer_Review : Counterparty accepts\nor submits counter-proposal

Reinsurer_Review --> Counterparty_Sign : Approved (all levels)

Counterparty_Sign --> Cycle_Sealed : Counter-signed\n[Audit ledger sealed — immutable]

Cycle_Sealed --> [*]
@enduml
....

=== Audit Ledger Design

The audit ledger is the platform's trust anchor. It uses a dual-layer design: S3 Object Lock as the immutability guarantee and PostgreSQL as the queryable index.

**Dual-write semantics:** For every audit event, the application writes first to S3 (Object Lock Compliance Mode), then commits the PostgreSQL audit row. The S3 object key and ETag are stored on the PostgreSQL row. The S3 write must succeed before the enclosing database transaction is committed — an S3 failure causes the transaction to roll back. A PostgreSQL write failure is non-fatal: a background reconciliation job rebuilds missing rows from S3. S3 is the system of record; PostgreSQL is the query layer.

**Why S3 Object Lock in addition to the hash-chain:** The hash-chain detects tampering within 7 days. S3 Object Lock in Compliance Mode makes tampering physically impossible — no IAM principal including account root can delete or overwrite a locked object within the retention period. For Solvency II Art. 259, "tamper-impossible" is a materially stronger answer than "tamper-detectable."

The PostgreSQL audit schema is a separate append-only schema (`audit`) within the same Aurora Serverless v2 instance, with distinct privileges:

* The application role has `INSERT` only — no `UPDATE`, no `DELETE`
* A dedicated verification role has `SELECT` only
* Database superusers are restricted by IAM policy; access requires a break-glass procedure logged in CloudTrail

Each event row stores the event type, acting user, a JSONB payload with event-specific data, two hash fields (`previous_hash`, `event_hash`) that form the per-tenant chain, and the S3 object key and ETag for the corresponding immutable S3 object. Row-Level Security isolates tenants at the database layer. The full schema definition — including privilege grants, RLS policies, and hash-chain linking logic — is delivered as part of the Phase 1 database migration scripts.

**Per-tenant hash chain:** Each tenant has an independent chain. Row N's `previous_hash` references the hash of the preceding event for the *same* `tenant_id`, not the globally preceding row. This allows concurrent month-end submissions from all counterparties without serialization contention.

**KMS-signed genesis:** When a tenant is provisioned, a genesis audit event (`TENANT_PROVISIONED`) is written whose `previous_hash` is a signature produced by AWS KMS (using a CMK dedicated to audit integrity). The full KMS key version ARN (not just the key ID) is stored on the genesis event row. This anchors the chain cryptographically — an attacker who deletes and re-inserts all rows cannot forge the genesis signature without access to the KMS key, which is controlled by IAM policy and logged in CloudTrail.

**Tamper detection:** A scheduled verification job running inside the application service recomputes each row's `event_hash` and checks that each `previous_hash` matches the preceding row's hash for that tenant. The job runs on every read of a sealed cycle (zero-cost at monthly reconciliation volume) and also on a weekly full-chain sweep. Any discrepancy triggers an immediate alert to the compliance team via SNS. The verification job uses the stored KMS key version ARN (from the genesis row) when calling `kms:Verify` — not the current default key version. Without this, the first CMK rotation after go-live causes false-positive `CHAIN_VIOLATION_DETECTED` alerts for all tenants provisioned before the rotation.

**Key design points:**

* **tenants** — each counterparty is a tenant with a designated data residency zone; Row-Level Security isolates all downstream data
* **contracts** — versioned contract definitions with expression tree rules stored as JSONB; `contract_file_types` defines which file types each contract requires; a trigger-based history table (via the `temporal_tables` PostgreSQL extension) with `valid_from`/`valid_to` columns enables "what were the contract terms on date X?" as a single query
* **reconciliation_cycles** — one cycle per contract per period; locks a `contract_version` at opening time (ADR-009); tracks workflow status via the `workflow_state` column (`AWAITING_FILES → AWAITING_ELIGIBILITY → AWAITING_L1 → AWAITING_L2 → AWAITING_COUNTERPARTY → COMPLETED / DISPUTED / ELIGIBILITY_FAILED`); a trigger-based history table (via the `temporal_tables` extension) preserves the full mutation history of each cycle record
* **cycle_files** — typed file uploads (people table, money movement, etc.) with SHA-256 checksums; includes `normalisation_mapping_version` (text, not null) recording which parser/mapping version normalised the counterparty file into the canonical format — required for Solvency II Art. 259 reproducibility: without this field, a parser update makes historical eligibility calculations unreproducible; drives the cycle readiness check
* **eligibility_results** — engine output with a generated `compensation_amount` column derived from the result JSONB; records engine version for reproducibility
* **approval_steps** — ordered sequence of L1/L2 approvals, adjustments, and counter-proposals within a cycle
* **adjustments** — cross-cycle correction chain tracked via `prior_cycle_id`, `root_cycle_id`, and `generation` (ADR-008)
* **audit.events** — append-only ledger with per-tenant SHA-256 hash chain; KMS-signed genesis anchor; no UPDATE or DELETE permitted

=== Eligibility Engine — Rule Schema

Contract rules are stored as structured expression trees validated against a versioned JSON Schema. The eligibility engine evaluates `eligibility_rule` as a boolean expression tree and `compensation_rule` as a computation tree — both without any contract-specific code. New field types (mortality rate lookup, annuity factor table) are added once to the evaluator, then usable across all contracts without per-contract changes. Each rule set contains a `schema_version` field so the engine knows which interpreter to use; unknown node types are rejected at contract upload time.

**Expression tree node types (initial set):**

* `AND` / `OR` — logical combinators; evaluate child conditions
* `NOT` — logical negation of a single child condition
* `range` — field value within `[min, max]`; supports open-ended ranges
* `in` — field value in a set of allowed values
* `eq` — exact match on a single value
* `tiered` — stepped rate table; selects rate based on the first matching tier
* `flat` — fixed rate per individual (simplest case)

New node types (e.g. `lookup` for mortality tables, `formula` for actuarial calculations) are added to the evaluator once and immediately usable in any contract definition without deployment changes.

**Complexity ceiling gate:** If the Investigation Period finds that more than 20% of contract types require node types not in the initial set (e.g. mortality table lookups, actuarial factor calculations, multi-dimensional tiered rates), the expression tree approach is escalated to a constrained formula DSL before Phase 2 begins. The escalation decision is a Phase 1→2 gate item — it is not deferred.

**Decimal precision:** All monetary values, rates, and factors in contract rule JSON are represented as strings, not JSON numbers, to prevent IEEE 754 rounding artefacts. The JSON Schema enforces a decimal string pattern; the eligibility engine parses strings into language-native exact decimal types at evaluation time.

**Validation and regression:** The engine validates rule JSON against a versioned JSON Schema at upload time. During Phase 1, the engine is run against 12 months of historical Excel output for 2–3 representative contracts. A pass requires 100% agreement on eligibility flags and compensation amounts before production use.

=== Testing Approach

* **Expression tree evaluator unit tests:** Every node type (AND, OR, range, tiered, flat, etc.) has a dedicated test suite; every contract rule has a corresponding test vector (input record → expected eligibility flag); side-by-side validation against existing Excel output used during Phase 1 workshops
* **Decimal precision tests:** Verify compensation calculations produce exact decimal results matching Excel output to the penny; no IEEE 754 rounding artefacts
* **Eligibility regression tests:** Engine output compared to 12 months of historical Excel results for 2–3 representative counterparties before Phase 2 go-ahead (Phase 1→2 gate)
* **Multi-file ingestion tests:** Verify cycle readiness logic — eligibility engine only triggers when all required file types are present; partial submissions do not trigger premature calculations
* **Multi-level approval tests:** Full cycle with L1 and L2 approvers; counter-proposal and revised file submission flows; verify all transitions produce correct audit events
* **RLS penetration tests:** Automated suite that attempts cross-tenant data access via API and direct DB connection; runs on every deployment
* **Hash-chain integrity tests:** Test suite that inserts events, tampers with one, and verifies the verification job detects the break per tenant; also validates dual-write (S3 Object Lock + PostgreSQL row) and the background rebuild path when a PostgreSQL row is missing
* **ECS deployment tests:** Verify all API endpoints respond correctly when deployed to ECS Fargate; verify ALB health checks and task startup time within acceptable limits for portal interactions
* **Month-end load test:** Concurrent file submission simulation (20 counterparties, multiple file types each) run against staging before each Phase go-live
* **Counterparty UAT:** First counterparty completes a full test cycle with synthetic data before live cycle approval

== Option 3: Event-Sourced Architecture

=== Overview

[cols="1,2"]
|===
|Timeline |{opt3-timeline} months
|CAPEX |{opt3-capex-approx} (incl. 25% contingency)
|OPEX / month |{opt3-opex-range}
|Team |{opt3-team}
|Counterparty scale |Unlimited
|Audit strength |Maximum — every state transition is a first-class immutable event; historical state is fully reconstructible by replaying the event log
|===

=== Approach

All state transitions are modelled as immutable domain events stored in an append-only event store (PostgreSQL + S3 event archive). The current state of any reconciliation cycle is derived by replaying its event log — there is no mutable state table. Read projections (materialised views or separate read models) serve query traffic.

This provides the strongest possible audit semantics: the event log *is* the audit ledger; tamper detection requires no hash chain because the event store schema is inherently append-only. However, it introduces significant architectural complexity:

* Engineers must think in events, not entities — a different mental model than CRUD
* Queries require projection tables that must be rebuilt if projections change
* Operational tooling for event replay and projection rebuild must be built and maintained
* Debugging requires event log inspection tools

=== When to Choose This Option

Option 3 becomes appropriate when:

* The counterparty portfolio grows beyond 50 and the application state machine's cycle volume or branching complexity justifies extraction to a managed workflow engine
* Regulators require full event-log replay capability (not just hash-chain verification)
* The team has existing event sourcing experience and tooling investment is justified

The recommended migration path from Option 2 to Option 3 is to introduce an event bus (Amazon EventBridge) alongside the existing hash-chain ledger, publishing events for new cycles while keeping existing cycles on the existing model — a gradual, non-disruptive evolution.

== Risks & Assumptions

=== Key Risks

[cols="2,1,1,3"]
|===
|Risk |Likelihood |Impact |Mitigation

|**Excel formula extraction complexity** — reconciliation managers claim contract logic is too complex to migrate to code
|Medium |High |Engage managers as domain experts in Phase 1 workshops; build rule-by-rule with side-by-side validation against Excel output; prior reinsurance projects have successfully migrated similar "dark Excel magic"

|**Counterparty onboarding friction** — external technical contacts are slow to engage or have legacy file format constraints
|Medium |Medium |Provide SFTP (AWS Transfer Family) as fallback exchange channel; assign a dedicated onboarding engineer per counterparty for the first wave

|**RLS misconfiguration** — a bug in PostgreSQL RLS policies could expose cross-tenant data
|Low |Critical |Automated RLS penetration test suite verifying tenant isolation on every deployment; separate read-only DB user per tenant; alert on any cross-tenant query observed in query logs

|**Regulatory interpretation gap** — FCA / Solvency II audit requirements may be more specific than assumed
|Low |High |Engage compliance lead in Phase 1; validate audit ledger design against Solvency II Article 259 record-keeping requirements before Phase 2 build begins

|**Key-person risk** — reconciliation managers hold undocumented contract formula knowledge
|High |Medium |Domain knowledge extraction sprint in Phase 1 produces documented, version-controlled rule sets; the platform itself removes the dependency on individuals holding formula knowledge in private Excel files

|**Duplicate file submission** — a counterparty re-uploads a file for a period already in progress (network retry, human error)
|Medium |High |FR-06a enforces a unique constraint on `(cycle_id, file_type)` before any S3 write or workflow start; the API returns HTTP 409 with a reference to the existing submission; prevents duplicate audit events for the same cycle

|**Eligibility computation for very large counterparty files** — files with >500K individuals could cause long-running computation within the ECS task
|Low |Low |Implement chunked processing inside the eligibility engine module: split input into batches and process sequentially or in parallel within the task; at initial scale (10–30 counterparties) a single pass suffices; ECS tasks have no 15-minute limit

|**Aurora Serverless v2 cold start** — database may take several seconds to scale up from minimum ACU after idle period
|Low |Low |Minimum ACU set to 0.5 (database is never fully cold); ECS Fargate tasks maintain persistent connections with bounded pool size; month-end peak is predictable — schedule a keep-warm DB query 1 hour before expected submission window

|**Data residency enforcement** — international counterparties may require data localisation in jurisdictions not covered by eu-west-2
|Low |Medium |`data_residency_zone` field on tenants table; Phase 1 all tenants use UK zone; when a non-UK/EU zone is needed, deploy an additional regional stack using the same Terraform module; contract and audit data stored exclusively in the tenant's zone
|===

=== Regulatory Compliance Gap Analysis

[cols="2,3,3", options="header"]
|===
|Regulation |Gap in current design |Proposed handling

|**Solvency II Pillar III — Article 259**
|Article 259 requires a documented audit trail of actuarial computations, including calculation inputs and outputs. The hash-chain ledger provides tamper evidence but does not explicitly define the granularity of `ELIGIBILITY_COMPUTED` payload content.
|The `ELIGIBILITY_COMPUTED` audit event payload must include: input file SHA-256, contract rule version, `normalisation_mapping_version`, per-individual eligibility flags, and the total compensation amount. The exact schema is to be confirmed with the compliance team in the Phase 1 compliance workshop.

|**FCA SYSC 9.1**
|SYSC 9.1 requires records of all client-facing communications. The current design logs file submissions and approval actions but does not explicitly capture negotiation messages (adjustment requests and free-text responses) in the audit ledger.
|`ADJUSTMENT_REQUESTED` and `ADJUSTMENT_ACCEPTED` events must include the full adjustment note text in their `payload`. Free-text negotiation messages entered via the portal are appended to the audit ledger as `COMMUNICATION_RECORDED` events at send time.

|**GDPR Article 17 — Right to Erasure**
|The append-only audit ledger cannot delete records. If counterparty employees' personal data (names, email addresses) are stored inline in audit event payloads, a Right to Erasure request cannot be fulfilled without breaking the hash chain.
|Personal identifiers (user name, email) are stored only in the mutable `users` table with a reference `actor_id` UUID. Audit event payloads contain only the UUID, never the raw personal data. On a Right to Erasure request, the user record is anonymised in the `users` table; the UUID reference in audit events remains intact and the chain is unaffected.
|===

=== Key Assumptions

* Counterparty count at launch is in the range of 10–30; RLS-based multi-tenancy is sufficient without schema-per-tenant
* Monthly cycle is the primary cadence; quarterly and annual cycles use the same workflow with a different `period` field — no separate code path required
* SAML 2.0 federation with a corporate IdP is not required for Phase 1; Cognito User Pools with MFA is sufficient; SAML federation is a Phase 2 option when a specific counterparty IT team requires enterprise IdP integration
* Budget is sufficient for Option 2 ({capex-approx} CAPEX, {tco-range-approx} {tco-years}-year TCO); client has confirmed budget is not the primary constraint for this innovation initiative
* Regulatory retention of 10 years satisfies the Solvency II run-off period for the contracts in scope — to be validated with the compliance team during the Phase 1 compliance workshop
* The development team includes backend engineers with experience deploying to ECS Fargate with a language that supports exact decimal arithmetic; specific language to be confirmed during the Investigation Period based on team capabilities
* All Phase 1 tenants are UK/EU-based; data residency zones beyond `UK` and `EU` are not needed until counterparty expansion to APAC or Americas

== Architecture Decisions

=== ADR-001: Immutability — Dual-Layer Audit (S3 Object Lock + PostgreSQL Hash Chain)

*Context:* The platform must provide tamper-evident records that satisfy FCA and Solvency II audit requirements. Options evaluated: blockchain, AWS QLDB, immuDB (Go-based), PostgreSQL with append-only pattern and hash chain, S3 Object Lock, and full event sourcing.

*Decision:* Dual-layer audit. S3 Object Lock Compliance Mode = immutability guarantee (primary, tamper-impossible). PostgreSQL hash-chain = query index (secondary, rebuildable from S3).

*Write semantics:* S3 write must succeed before the PostgreSQL audit row is committed. The S3 object key and ETag are stored on the audit row. PostgreSQL index failure is non-fatal — a background reconciliation job rebuilds missing rows from S3. S3 write failure causes the enclosing transaction to roll back. S3 is the system of record; PostgreSQL is the query layer.

*Rationale:*
* **Why S3 Object Lock in addition to the hash-chain:** The hash-chain detects tampering within 7 days. S3 Object Lock in Compliance Mode makes tampering physically impossible — no IAM principal including account root can delete or overwrite a locked object within the retention period. For Solvency II Art. 259, "tamper-impossible" is a materially stronger answer than "tamper-detectable."
* **Blockchain** rejected — the reinsurer is the sole custodian of this platform; blockchain's value is distributed consensus between mutually distrusting parties. A single custodian gains nothing from consensus overhead and inherits all of the governance and key-management complexity.
* **AWS QLDB** rejected — discontinued by AWS in 2025; long-term viability cannot be assured. The underlying cryptographic model (hash chain over a Merkle tree) is sound, but the same model can be implemented directly in PostgreSQL without vendor lock-in.
* **immuDB** rejected — despite sound architecture, consistency and transaction management issues emerged in a prior production project integrating from a non-Go application layer; migrating away required significant rework. The risk of opaque internals in a trust-critical system is not acceptable.
* **Full event sourcing** deferred — architecturally superior for auditability but adds projection rebuild complexity and requires specialist knowledge the initial team does not have. Deferred to Option 3 migration when counterparty volume justifies it.
* **PostgreSQL hash chain** retained as the query layer — regulators can query it with standard SQL; SHA-256 verification is transparent and reproducible by any auditor; the team already operates PostgreSQL; `pgaudit` adds DB-level statement logging as defence-in-depth. The chain is partitioned per tenant to eliminate write serialization at month-end; a KMS-signed genesis anchor prevents undetected chain reconstruction.

=== ADR-002: Multi-Tenancy — Row-Level Security

*Context:* The platform serves multiple independent counterparty insurers who must be strictly isolated from each other. Options: schema-per-tenant, row-level security (RLS), separate databases per tenant.

*Decision:* PostgreSQL Row-Level Security enforced at the database layer; all tenants share a single schema; `app.current_tenant_id` set via `SET LOCAL` (transaction-scoped) by the API service at the start of every database transaction.

*Rationale:* Schema-per-tenant provides the strongest isolation but adds significant migration complexity as counterparty count grows (running schema migrations across 30 schemas is operationally painful). Separate databases per tenant would make cross-tenant admin queries (for the platform operator) impractical. RLS is the pragmatic middle ground — proven in multi-tenant SaaS at this scale, with the additional safety net of WAF rules and API-layer tenant checks.

`SET LOCAL` is used instead of `SET` so that the tenant context is transaction-scoped and automatically cleared when the transaction ends. This prevents the known production failure mode where a connection pool reuses a session before the session variable is cleared — which would silently expose the prior tenant's data to the next request on that connection.

=== ADR-003: Approval Workflow — Application-Layer State Machine

*Context:* The multi-level approval chain (propose → L1 reinsurer review → L2 senior review → adjustment rounds → counterparty counter-proposal or revised file → counter-sign) needs durable state management with human-approval steps that can pause for hours or days. The workflow must support a chain of 2–4+ approvers per cycle and allow the counterparty to re-submit revised data files at any point before seal.

*Decision:* Application-layer state machine implemented within the Approval Workflow module. The `reconciliation_cycles` table has a `workflow_state` column tracking states: `AWAITING_FILES → AWAITING_ELIGIBILITY → AWAITING_L1 → AWAITING_L2 → AWAITING_COUNTERPARTY → COMPLETED / DISPUTED / ELIGIBILITY_FAILED`. A background job runner (running inside the ECS Fargate service) handles the 72-hour escalation timer. Other modules call `ApprovalWorkflow.transition(cycleId, event)` — a clean interface that allows extraction to Step Functions later if the workflow grows beyond ~5 concurrent workflow types or multi-week execution lifetimes.

*Rationale:*
* **Step Functions** was designed to orchestrate Lambda functions across service boundaries. With a modular monolith, those boundaries no longer exist.
* At 15–20 counterparties × 12 cycles/year = 180–240 workflows/year, an application state machine with a `workflow_state` column eliminates Step Functions IAM complexity, task token management, and callback patterns at no functional cost.
* Durable execution state is already provided by the PostgreSQL `reconciliation_cycles` row — no external workflow engine is needed to persist state between human actions.
* The clean `ApprovalWorkflow.transition(cycleId, event)` interface makes future extraction to Step Functions an additive change, not a rework.
* The hash-chain audit ledger remains the *sole compliance archive*; workflow state transitions are application events written to the ledger, not execution history in an external service.

=== ADR-004: File Exchange — S3 Pre-Signed URLs with Typed Multi-File Ingestion

*Context:* Counterparties need to submit monthly data files securely. The requirements describe five distinct file types per reconciliation cycle (people tables, money movement tables, special condition tables, adjustment records, contract exceptions). Options: SFTP-only, web upload via S3 pre-signed URLs, API-based upload, email attachment (current state).

*Decision:* Web portal upload via S3 pre-signed URLs as the primary channel; AWS Transfer Family SFTP as an opt-in secondary channel. Each upload is tagged with a file type; the eligibility engine is triggered only when all required file types for a contract have been submitted (tracked via `cycle_readiness` view).

*Rationale:* Most counterparty contacts are non-technical users who interact with a web portal; SFTP-only would require client software and firewall coordination. Pre-signed URLs allow the browser to upload directly to S3 without proxying through the API service (better performance, lower cost, no file size limits from API gateway). SFTP is retained as a fallback to avoid blocking counterparties with legacy automation. The typed ingestion model matches real-world practice where counterparties submit different file types at different times during the month — a generic single-file upload would either trigger incomplete calculations or force counterparties to bundle all file types into one upload.

=== ADR-005: Authentication — Cognito User Pools with MFA; SAML Deferred

*Context:* The platform serves two user populations: internal reinsurer staff (who may have a corporate identity provider) and external counterparty administrators (who do not have a shared IdP).

*Decision:* Cognito User Pools with email + MFA for Phase 1. SAML 2.0 federation is available as a Phase 2 addition when a specific counterparty IT team requires enterprise IdP integration. The Cognito User Pool is configured with an IdP placeholder to make this addition a configuration change, not a code change. Both paths issue JWTs from one issuer; a `custom:user_type` claim (`INTERNAL` or `COUNTERPARTY`) drives RBAC in the API service.

*Rationale:* SAML federation setup requires metadata exchange with the corporate IT team, which is a coordination dependency the platform build should not block on. Cognito User Pools with MFA is sufficient for all Phase 1 users — internal staff included. The IdP placeholder means the federation is a one-day configuration task whenever a specific counterparty requires it. Cognito MFA is enforced for all users regardless of the authentication path.

=== ADR-006: Compute — ECS Fargate Modular Monolith + Aurora Serverless v2

*Context:* The workload is monthly peaks with near-zero baseline between reconciliation cycles (a few portal logins per week). The architecture is a modular monolith. Options: ECS Fargate (container tasks behind ALB), Lambda + API Gateway (pay-per-invocation), EKS (Kubernetes).

*Decision:* Single ECS Fargate service hosting the entire modular monolith (API + eligibility engine + background jobs), fronted by an Application Load Balancer. Aurora Serverless v2 for the database.

*Rationale:*

* **Lambda** rejected — the modular monolith architecture eliminates the need for function-level granularity. The original Fargate rejection (~$380/month idle cost) was based on a multi-service microservices model. A single Fargate task (0.5 vCPU / 1 GB) costs ~$18/month; two tasks for HA ~$35/month; month-end scaled to 4 tasks ~$52/month. Connection pooling to Aurora is deterministic (bounded task count × pool size). No Lambda VPC ENI exhaustion at month-end. No 15-minute execution limit. Single container image, single deployment pipeline, consistent local dev environment.
* **Aurora Serverless v2** chosen over RDS fixed-instance — scales to near-zero ACUs (0.5 ACU minimum ≈ 1 GB RAM) between peaks. At month-end, it scales automatically to handle concurrent eligibility computations without any capacity planning. RLS, pgaudit, and the hash-chain audit ledger work identically on Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible. Monthly cost: ~$200 vs ~$480 for RDS db.r6g.large.
* **EKS** rejected — operational overhead of managing a Kubernetes cluster is not justified for a {team-size}-person team with a monthly-peak workload.

WARNING: RDS Proxy is not used in this deployment (see ADR-010). At 2–4 Fargate tasks, the connection count is bounded and predictable. Revisit if task count exceeds 10.

=== ADR-007: Contract Rules — Structured Expression Tree

*Context:* The platform must accept contract definitions as structured metadata without constraining contract authors to a rigid schema that breaks when a new contract type is introduced. Options: flat JSON with code-per-contract, expression tree with generic evaluator, embedded DSL (e.g. SpEL/MVEL), Rete-based rule engine.

*Decision:* Contract rules stored as a structured expression tree evaluated by a generic engine. Validated against a versioned JSON Schema at upload time. See the _Eligibility Engine — Rule Schema_ section for the node type taxonomy and decimal precision approach.

*Rationale:*

* **Flat JSON** rejected — breaks when a contract has stepped rates by age band, multi-condition eligibility, or annuity factor tables. Every new contract type would require a code change.
* **Expression tree** chosen — the engine evaluates eligibility and compensation rules as tree structures without contract-specific code. New node types are added once to the evaluator, then usable across all contracts. A `schema_version` field ensures reproducibility.
* **Embedded DSL (SpEL/MVEL)** rejected — creates a security risk (arbitrary code execution) and makes audit reproducibility harder.
* **Rete-based rule engine (Drools)** rejected — operational overhead not justified at this scale.

=== ADR-008: Adjustment Reconciliation — Snapshot-Based Model

*Context:* Corrections from prior months are folded into subsequent cycles as explicit adjustment records. When month 3 adjusts month 1, and month 5 adjusts month 3's adjustment of month 1, the platform must define how multi-generation adjustment chains affect eligibility calculations and audit reproducibility. Options: delta-based (each adjustment is a differential applied to the prior result) or snapshot-based (each adjustment is a self-contained recalculation from the original data).

*Decision:* Snapshot-based adjustment model. Each adjustment record triggers a full eligibility recalculation using the original cycle's data files plus the adjustment parameters. The result is a complete, self-contained eligibility snapshot — not a delta applied to the prior result.

*Rationale:*

* **Delta-based** rejected — applying sequential deltas requires replaying the full adjustment chain to reconstruct the current state. If any intermediate delta is incorrect, all downstream deltas propagate the error. Debugging requires understanding every delta in the chain, which reintroduces the same person-dependent knowledge problem the platform is designed to eliminate.
* **Snapshot-based** chosen — each adjustment produces a complete result that can be verified independently. An auditor reconstructing the state of a contract at month 3 reads a single `ELIGIBILITY_COMPUTED` event with full inputs and outputs — no chain replay required. The `adjustments` table's `prior_cycle_id` and `root_cycle_id` fields provide traceability back to the originating cycle, but the eligibility result at each generation is self-contained.
* The `generation` field on the `adjustments` table tracks the depth of the chain (generation 0 = original, generation 1 = first correction, etc.). The `ELIGIBILITY_COMPUTED` audit event payload includes the `root_cycle_id` and `generation` so the full correction history is traceable from any point in the chain.
* Trade-off: snapshot recalculations are more compute-expensive than deltas, but at monthly cadence with Lambda's pay-per-invocation model, the cost is negligible.

=== ADR-009: Contract Version Locking at Cycle Opening

*Context:* Contract rules can be updated between reconciliation cycles (e.g. renegotiated terms, corrected parameters). If a contract version changes after a counterparty has uploaded files but before the cycle is signed off, the platform must determine which rule version applies.

*Decision:* Eligibility computation is locked to the contract version that was active at cycle opening time. The `reconciliation_cycles` table records a `contract_version_id` at cycle creation. Mid-cycle contract changes apply to the next cycle only.

*Rationale:* Both parties' expectations for a cycle are set when the cycle opens. Applying a mid-cycle rule change would invalidate work already reviewed by the counterparty and create a dispute trigger. The locked version is recorded in the audit ledger alongside every `ELIGIBILITY_COMPUTED` event, ensuring reproducibility. If a rule correction is genuinely needed for the current cycle, the existing flow supports it: close the current cycle as voided, open a new cycle with the corrected contract version, and re-upload files — all captured in the audit trail.

=== ADR-010: RDS Proxy — Deferred

*Context:* RDS Proxy is a standard mitigation for database connection exhaustion when a large number of compute functions compete for a limited connection pool. It is commonly paired with Lambda deployments and with RLS to manage `SET LOCAL` session variable scoping.

*Decision:* RDS Proxy is not used in the initial deployment.

*Rationale:*
* At 15–20 counterparties with a bounded ECS Fargate task count (2–4 tasks), the maximum concurrent database connections is predictable and well within Aurora Serverless v2 limits.
* RDS Proxy is the standard mitigation for Lambda connection exhaustion — that problem no longer applies with Fargate.
* RDS Proxy with RLS requires transaction-pinning mode (to prevent `SET LOCAL` session variable leakage across multiplexed connections), which adds configuration complexity with no benefit at this connection volume.
* Revisit when Fargate task count exceeds 10 or counterparty count exceeds 50.

=== Security Controls

[cols="2,3"]
|===
|Control |Approach

|Authentication |Single Cognito User Pool; Cognito-native (email/password + MFA) for Phase 1 all users; SAML 2.0 federation available as Phase 2 addition via pre-configured IdP placeholder; MFA enforced for all users
|Authorisation |Role-based access control (RBAC) with five roles spanning reinsurer, counterparty, compliance, and platform administration. Every approval action (L1 approve, L2 approve, counter-proposal, final sign-off) enforces three checks in the application layer: (1) re-validate the caller's Cognito JWT, (2) confirm the approver's role matches the required approval level for this action, (3) confirm the target cycle belongs to the caller's tenant. Authentication alone (valid JWT) is not sufficient — all three checks must pass before any state transition is executed.
|Data isolation |PostgreSQL RLS at DB layer; transaction-scoped tenant context to prevent connection-pool bleed; WAF rate limiting attached to ALB
|Encryption |AES-256 at rest (KMS-managed); TLS 1.2+ in transit; dedicated KMS CMK for audit-critical data; S3 audit bucket uses SSE-KMS with the audit CMK
|Network security |ECS Fargate tasks in private subnets; Aurora not publicly accessible; WAF (ALB-attached) with OWASP managed rule group
|S3 audit bucket controls |Bucket policy includes explicit Deny on `s3:DeleteObject` and `s3:PutObject` without Object Lock headers — prevents any principal (including account root) from bypassing Object Lock. S3 raw file bucket uses Object Lock Governance Mode (allows operator override with justification; enables non-repudiation if a counterparty disputes that the system altered their file).
|Audit logging |Three layers: AWS CloudTrail (API calls), database statement logging, application-level audit ledger (business events)
|Break-glass access |Superuser access requires documented procedure with alerting; all access logged
|===

=== Disaster Recovery

* **Strategy:** Primary in eu-west-2 (London); DR via automated daily snapshots to eu-west-1 (Ireland) via AWS Backup and S3 Cross-Region Replication. No active standby is maintained in eu-west-1.
* **Aurora Serverless v2:** Multi-AZ automatic failover within eu-west-2 (RTO ~1 min for AZ failure); AWS Backup cross-region snapshots to eu-west-1 (RPO = 24h for full region failure)
* **S3:** Cross-Region Replication to eu-west-1 with 15-minute SLA; versioning enabled in both regions
* **Audit Ledger:** Aurora Multi-AZ replication ensures audit events are synchronously replicated (RPO = 0 for AZ failure); S3 Object Lock audit objects are replicated via S3 CRR
* **ECS Fargate:** Stateless compute — no DR concern; the same container image and Terraform module are used to provision the DR region when a full-region restore is required
* **RTO target:** < 4 hours (snapshot restore) for full region failure; documented and tested DR restore runbook; maintenance windows scheduled outside month-end submission periods

NOTE: Target 99.9% monthly uptime. Expected availability based on component SLA product (Aurora Multi-AZ × ECS Fargate × ALB) is ~99.85%. The gap between target and expected is addressed by scheduling maintenance windows outside month-end submission periods.

== Post-Launch Plan

=== Hypercare (Weeks 1–4 after First Counterparty Go-Live)

The first four weeks after go-live include daily stand-ups with the reinsurer IT and reconciliation ops team, a 24/7 on-call rota for the first month-end submission window, a dedicated channel with the first counterparty’s technical contact, and side-by-side eligibility result validation against a parallel Excel run for the first two cycles.

=== Counterparty Integration Tiers

Counterparties vary in technical capability. The platform supports three integration tiers; the tier is agreed during onboarding and can be upgraded at any time.

[cols="1,2,2,2", options="header"]
|===
|Tier |Profile |Authentication |File Exchange

|**Tier 1 — Federated** (Phase 2)
|Large insurer with corporate SSO requiring enterprise IdP integration
|SAML 2.0 federation from counterparty IdP into the platform Cognito User Pool (Phase 2 addition via pre-configured IdP placeholder; configuration change only)
|Web portal upload via S3 pre-signed URLs

|**Tier 2 — Portal**
|Smaller insurer; no corporate IdP
|Cognito-native email/password with mandatory MFA (TOTP or SMS)
|Web portal upload via S3 pre-signed URLs

|**Tier 3 — File-based**
|Legacy counterparty with existing SFTP automation; no portal adoption
|Service account credentials for SFTP; no portal login required
|AWS Transfer Family SFTP (provisioned on-demand for this counterparty only)
|===

=== Counterparty Onboarding Runbook

1. Agree integration tier and provision IdP federation or SFTP endpoint as needed
2. Provision tenant (ID, name, country code, data residency zone) and upload contract definition with file type configuration
3. Configure file normalisation mapping: obtain a sample file, define column/format mappings, validate against canonical schema using the mapping validation tool
4. Verify rule parsing, file type configuration, and expression tree validation against JSON Schema
5. Provision counterparty user (Cognito invite + MFA setup, or SFTP service account)
6. Run synthetic test cycle end-to-end: file upload → normalisation → cycle readiness → eligibility → approval → counter-sign; UAT sign-off by counterparty and compliance lead
7. First live cycle in parallel with Excel for one month; decommission Excel on successful validation

=== Audit Ledger Health

* **On every sealed-cycle read:** hash chain recomputed for that tenant's cycle events at query time; any discrepancy returns an error before the data is returned
* **Weekly full-chain sweep:** scheduled verification job running inside the application service (same background job runner as escalation timers) recomputes all events per tenant for the rolling 7-day window; alerts compliance team via SNS on any discrepancy. The verification job must use the stored KMS key version ARN (from the genesis event row) when calling `kms:Verify` — not the current default key version. Without this, the first CMK rotation after go-live causes false-positive `CHAIN_VIOLATION_DETECTED` alerts for all tenants provisioned before the rotation.
* **Monthly full-chain verification** for regulatory assurance; output archived as compliance evidence
* **Quarterly compliance report:** cycle count, event count, verification pass rate, any anomalies

=== Platform Evolution Roadmap

The items below are outside the current engagement scope but are a direct extension of the architecture being built. They are documented here so that design decisions in Phases 1–4 do not inadvertently foreclose them.

NOTE: Three design disciplines preserve optionality at zero additional cost: no client-specific hardcoding anywhere in the platform, the file normalisation component behind a `FileNormaliser` interface (so an API-based adapter can replace it without rebuilding ingestion), and metered usage logging from day one (required for future SaaS billing).

[cols="2,3,2,2", options="header"]
|===
|Capability |What it adds |Prerequisites |Earliest realistic timing

|**Counterparty self-service data quality portal**
|Pre-submission validation API: counterparties run the platform's schema and sanity checks against their file before the official upload cycle opens; self-remediate data quality issues upstream of the reconciliation workflow; reduces dispute rate from day one
|Phase 2 ingestion and normalisation pipeline complete; validation logic exposed as a read-only API endpoint
|Phase 4 scope extension — approximately 2 months additional effort; high ROI relative to cost

|**ML anomaly detection**
|Statistical baseline per counterparty portfolio; flag mortality submissions that deviate significantly from historical norms before they enter the eligibility engine; surface data quality errors and potential fraud early without human review
|12–18 months of per-counterparty historical data; read-replica analytics store; anonymised data pipeline (GDPR review required for cross-counterparty aggregation)
|18–24 months post-launch; revisit at Phase 4 retrospective

|**Platform commercialisation (SaaS)**
|White-label and offer to other longevity reinsurers; the multi-tenant architecture, configurable contract rules, and per-counterparty file normalisation already constitute a SaaS product; converts the platform from a cost centre to a revenue stream
|SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 certification; self-service tenant onboarding; usage metering and billing integration; product support structure
|24+ months post-launch; earliest review at 12-month post-go-live retrospective

== Next Steps

1. Share this design with reinsurer leadership and compliance lead for review; obtain sign-off before Phase 1 procurement
2. Validate audit ledger design against Solvency II Article 259 record-keeping requirements with the compliance team — confirm 10-year retention period and acceptable format for regulatory submissions
3. Schedule domain knowledge extraction workshops with reconciliation managers in Phase 1, Week 1 — identify the 3 most common contract types and build expression tree rule sets with side-by-side Excel validation
4. Confirm first counterparty for onboarding pilot and identify their technical contact; document which of the five file types (people tables, money movement, special conditions, adjustment records, contract exceptions) they submit and in what sequence
5. Procure AWS accounts (separate accounts for dev/staging/production recommended); set up AWS Organizations and Control Tower baseline
6. Evaluate backend language options during the Investigation Period — confirm a language with native exact decimal arithmetic support deployable to ECS Fargate; finalise the choice before Phase 1 sprint planning
7. Review and sign Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) with each counterparty before their data is processed on the platform (GDPR requirement for EU-based counterparties)
8. Confirm data residency requirements for all launch counterparties; assign residency zones (`UK` or `EU` for Phase 1)
